source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: GPS-I has three goal types and three methods. Goal 1: transform object a into b. Goal 2: apply operator q to a. Goal 3: reduce the difference d between a and b. Method 1 matches a to b, gets a difference, sets a Goal 3 to reduce it, then a new Goal 1 from the changed object c to b. Method 2 turns a into the operator's input form, then builds the output. Method 3 finds an operator relevant to the difference and tries it, and tries another if it fails. Before acting, a goal is checked for being worth the effort and likely to succeed.
numbers: Report dated 12-30-58, revised 2-9-59. Fig 2 shows the three methods. Domains shown: symbolic logic, trigonometry/algebra.
quote: Make progress by substituting for the achievement of a goal the achievement of a set of easier goals.
limits: Authors say the aim is a theory of human thinking, not an economical solver. Methods are fixed by hand. The report gives no timing or success-rate statistics.
agent_relevance: This is the exact loop behind our S6 operator choice: compare, name the difference, pick an operator by difference, set a subgoal for its preconditions. Code can run it; the model fills only the slot.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: The difference-to-operator link is a hand-made table of connections. The authors say GPS could infer the connections itself from the operator and difference lists, for example by finding that R1 swaps A and B and so relates to a position difference. Differences are also ranked by difficulty and used as the criterion of progress. The match step tests the more important differences first.
numbers: Difference types seen in the traces: position (dP), connective (dC), variable (-V), and a type dT. Fig 3 gives the table for logic.
quote: we provide criteria of progress, in terms of a list of the differences in order of difficulty.
limits: The table is domain knowledge supplied by people. Its quality decides everything. No test of how wrong a table can be.
agent_relevance: Our operators O1-O8 need an explicit table 'difference seen -> operator', plus a ranking of differences. We can log which row fired. Wrong rows are a failure source we can measure.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Worked logic trace: from L1 = R.(-P implies Q) to L0 = (Q or P).R. GPS finds a position difference, tries operator R1, finds a connective difference, tries R5, then R6, then R1 again. One candidate (goal 9) is rejected because its difference is no easier than the one in its parent goal (goal 6). This is the loop check: a subgoal must be easier than its ancestor.
numbers: 16 goals in total (Fig 4). Operators applied: R1, R6, R1. One goal rejected as 'no easier'.
quote: Goal rejected: difference is no easier than difference in Goal 6.
limits: One hand-picked example. No count of dead ends over a problem set.
agent_relevance: Rule to copy as code: reject a subgoal whose difference is not smaller or easier than its parent. It stops infinite goal recursion without asking the model.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Trigonometry trace: from (tan x + cot x) sin x cos x to 1. GPS removes tan, cot, cos, sin one at a time by variable differences, with several 'apply, no change produced' attempts, then combines terms to sin^2 + cos^2. In the conclusion the authors say GPS needs extra goals and methods for features, equations in one variable, and learned heuristics such as 'reduce everything to sines and cosines'; it followed these 'in a cumbersome fashion'.
numbers: 33 goals in the trace (Fig 6). About 5 operator attempts produced no change.
quote: it followed these roughly in the example given, but only in a cumbersome fashion.
limits: Success shown on worked examples chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Shows the cost of pure difference reduction: many wasted subgoals. Our schema should count wasted goals as a budget signal.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Second GPS heuristic, planning: drop detail from the problem (abstract), solve the abstract problem with the same means-ends loop, then use the abstract solution as a plan to guide the full problem. In the logic example it made several plans (P1 = R8,R11,R12; P2 = R8,R8,R12). P1 failed when translated back to the real problem; P2 worked. The authors count the time lost on invalid plans against the heuristic.
numbers: 25 goals in the planning trace (Fig 8). Two plans tried, one failed.
quote: The time wasted in fruitless efforts to execute invalid plans must be counted in evaluating the planning heuristic
limits: The authors say a plan may be 'illusory'. No rate of false plans given.
agent_relevance: Plan-then-check pattern: an abstract plan is only a hint (matches G3). Check each plan step against the real state before trusting it.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (RAND P-1584)
finding: Core design idea: separate problem-solving method from task content. 'General' means the same heuristics work on different subject matter once rules for that domain are supplied. All heuristics follow the principle of subgoal reduction. The authors note chess and checkers programs of that time did not use it, so it is a heuristic, not a law. A problem is defined as a desired state one does not immediately know how to reach.
numbers: Summary lists four features: recursion, content/technique separation, two techniques (means-ends, planning), memory organisation.
quote: The justification for calling GPS "general" lies in this factorization of problem-solving heuristics from subject matter
limits: The 'general' claim was argued by example only. Later work (a12, a15) shows its limits.
agent_relevance: Same split as our design: fixed program for method, swappable domain facts. Supports keeping the scaffold domain-free and putting task facts in slots.

source: Newell, Shaw & Simon (1958) Elements of a theory of human problem solving
finding: The Logic Theorist (LT), the program GPS grew out of, proved 38 of the first 52 theorems of Principia Mathematica chapter 2 using heuristics, not brute force. About half of the proofs took under a minute, most others 1 to 5 minutes, a few 15 to 45 minutes. Blind search of the same space would take 'hundreds or even thousands of years'. Removing earlier proved theorems from memory stopped LT from proving Theorem 2.12, which it proved in about 10 seconds with them.
numbers: 38/52 = 73% proved. Time grows sharply (perhaps exponentially) with proof length. Theorem 2.12: about 10 s with prior theorems, failed without.
quote: LT succeeded in proving 38 (73%) of the 52 theorems.
limits: Single program run on one problem set in one order. LT is not yet means-ends: it uses substitution, detachment, chaining, and similarity tests. The authors say success depends sensitively on problem order.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: heuristic guidance beats blind search by orders of magnitude, and success depends on what earlier results are kept in memory and in what order. Supports a shared store of solved subgoals.

source: Newell & Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry: symbols and search (Turing lecture)
finding: The authors define means-ends analysis as detecting specific differences between the current structure and the goal structure, then choosing actions relevant to reducing those differences. They say the General Problem Solver, embodying it, appeared about 1957 but combined it with modified depth-first rather than best-first search. They state that many GPS mechanisms came from protocols of people thinking aloud, and state the heuristic search hypothesis: symbol systems solve problems by generating and testing potential solutions.
numbers: No experiment numbers. Dates: Logic Theorist 1955 (rudiments of best-first search), GPS about 1957.
quote: employing a simple form of means-ends analysis to give direction to the search.
limits: A synthesis by the authors themselves, so it is advocacy as well as history.
agent_relevance: Gives the clean definition we can quote in the schema. Also reminds us that GPS search was depth-first with difference guidance, not best-first with a score.

source: Newell & Simon (1976) Computer science as empirical inquiry
finding: The paper says the amount of mathematical theory behind these search ideas is 'miniscule': some theorems on alpha-beta pruning, a couple on shortest-path search, and some on best-first search with probabilistic evaluation. It also says each technique was reinvented many times and task-independent theory of problem solving only appeared in the middle or late 1960s.
numbers: Counts of formal results: about 3 families named (alpha-beta, shortest path, probabilistic best-first). None for means-ends.
quote: The amount of formal buttressing they have received from mathematical theory is still miniscule
limits: Written in 1976; the later planning-theory results (a13, a34) are not covered.
agent_relevance: Means-ends analysis has no performance guarantee in the founding theory. Any gain we claim must be measured, not assumed.

source: Fikes & Nilsson (1971) STRIPS: a new approach to the application of theorem proving to problem solving (SRI TN 43 version)
finding: STRIPS is stated to be a combination of GPS and formal theorem proving. It keeps GPS's difference-and-relevant-operator strategy but builds the 'difference' from a theorem prover: it tries to prove the goal in the current world model, and clauses left over from the failed proof become the difference. Candidate operators are those whose add list can resolve with a difference clause. The search combines forward search (apply a relevant operator when its preconditions hold) and backward search (set preconditions as new goals), because a relevant operator may land at the start, middle or end of the plan.
numbers: Tree node form: (world model, goal list); the first goal on the list is the current subgoal. Differences are chosen by heuristics such as clause length and depth in proof tree.
quote: Thus it is fair to say that STRIPS is a combination of GPS and formal theorem-proving methods.
limits: Original 1970 tech note. Experiments are a robot example with objects and rooms. The paper gives no benchmark of solved problems.
agent_relevance: Direct template for O5: a difference can be the unproved leftover of a check, not just a feature comparison. Code can run the check; the leftover tells which operator is relevant.

source: Fikes & Nilsson (1971) STRIPS: a new approach to the application of theorem proving to problem solving (SRI TN 43 version)
finding: STRIPS fixes the frame problem by writing each operator as a precondition formula plus an add list and a delete list. Everything not deleted stays true. The authors store all world models in one shared memory with changes marked, because copying a full world model per node is infeasible for hundreds of wffs. In the closing section they propose, as future work, turning a found solution into a new generalised operator (macro operator) and say the main difficulty is generalising constants into parameters.
numbers: Delete list must name every atom to remove; the authors note this can delete clauses unnecessarily.
limits: The generalisation step is only proposed here; later systems carried it out (see a33).
agent_relevance: Add/delete lists are a cheap way to track what a step changes. Our subgoal library (memory) could store solved subgoals as operators with preconditions and effects.

source: Norvig (1992) Paradigms of AI Programming, chapter 4: GPS, the General Problem Solver
finding: A working re-implementation of GPS (after STRIPS) exposes named flaws. Clobbered sibling goal: to get the child to school and keep money, GPS buys a battery with the money and still reports SOLVED, because it only checks goals one after another, not that all still hold. Leaping before you look: planning and acting are interleaved, so GPS runs every action up to the dead end before it returns failure. Others named: running around the block (no net change, no reason to apply), lack of descriptive power (no variables, no costs, no time), perfect information, interacting goals.
numbers: Fix for clobbering: achieve-all checks that all goals still hold at the end. Goal order (have-money son-at-school) wrongly succeeds; order (son-at-school have-money) returns NIL only after executing all steps.
quote: In other words, no combination of plans for the two individual goals can solve the conjunction of the two goals.
limits: This is a teaching re-implementation, not the 1959 program. Flaws are shown on toy domains (nursery school, monkey and bananas, maze, blocks).
agent_relevance: Two code-checkable rules: after a plan, re-verify that all goals hold together (G3 style), and plan in a copy of the state, not on the real one.

source: Norvig (1992) PAIP chapter 4
finding: The Sussman anomaly: in the three-block problem (C on A, A and B on table; goal A on B and B on C) GPS returns NIL for both goal orders. No ordering of the two goals works, because achieving one goal as a step clobbers the other. This shows that treating conjunctive goals as independent subgoals is not enough. Norvig notes it leads to later planners (WARPLAN with protected goals, NONLIN, TWEAK).
numbers: Tested orders: 2 of 2 fail. Start state and goal given in the chapter section 'The Sussman Anomaly'.
limits: Original discovery was by Sussman (1975, HACKER); here only a reconstruction.
agent_relevance: If our task has several conjunctive goals, doing them one after another can fail whatever the order. Need an interleaving or re-check step. Flag as a test case.

source: Norvig (1992) PAIP chapter 4
finding: In the taxi variant (taxi costs the money), GPS cannot reach 'son at school AND have money' even though driving works, because achieve takes only the first operator that fits. Plan repair works in blocks and maze worlds because every step can be undone, but not here because spent money is gone. Two fixes: try all solutions (Prolog style) or keep a list of protected goals that no operator may delete.
numbers: One ordering fails; the other fails after repair; a solution (drive) exists but is never found.
quote: In domains like the block world and maze world, repair often works, because all steps are reversible.
limits: Toy example. Protection alone still needs search over orderings.
agent_relevance: Mark irreversible steps. Where a step cannot be undone, check the preconditions and side effects before acting. Matches the rule 'revise only from real output' since revision needs reversibility.

source: Norvig (1992) PAIP chapter 4
finding: Norvig's verdict: GPS is general only in that the domain is swapped by changing the operator list; it fails to solve many interesting problems and is confined to small tricks and games. He points to combinatorial blow-up (NP-hard problems) as the deeper reason, and says modern solvers limit the problem class, accept partial answers, or monitor their own time and give up. He quotes McDermott that GPS should have been named a 'Local Feature-Guided Network Searcher'. He also notes means-ends is a choice: forward or mixed search is possible.
numbers: No experiment numbers.
quote: It is not a very general problem solver at all.
limits: Opinion of a textbook author; consistent with Newell and Simon's own admission (a09).
agent_relevance: Do not expect a general gain from means-ends alone. Add a time and goal budget and a give-up rule (adaptive stopping subfield).

source: Veloso, Carbonell, Perez, Borrajo, Fink & Blythe (1995) Integrating planning and learning: the PRODIGY architecture
url: local copy of the journal paper (CMU PRODIGY group, JETAI 1995); no stable URL recorded
finding: PRODIGY4.0 is a complete nonlinear planner that 'follows a means-ends analysis backward chaining search procedure'. An unfinished plan has a head-plan (steps already simulated forward from the start state) and a tail-plan (steps chained backward from the goal). Each step either adds an operator to the tail by backward chaining or moves an applicable operator from tail to head. So it mixes goal-directed chaining with forward state simulation. Control is steered by select, reject and prefer rules at each decision point.
numbers: Decision points steered by control rules: choice of goal, operator, bindings, and apply-or-subgoal. Versions: PRODIGY2.0 linear and incomplete, PRODIGY4.0 nonlinear and complete.
quote: It follows a means-ends analysis backward chaining search procedure reasoning about multiple goals and multiple alternative operators relevant to achieving the goals.
limits: Review by the authors of their own system. It reports their domain tests, not independent ones.
agent_relevance: Gives a working design: backward chaining to find needed steps, forward simulation to know the real state, and explicit control rules that can be learned. Control rules map to our code-checked transitions.

source: Veloso, Carbonell, Perez, Borrajo, Fink & Blythe (1995) Integrating planning and learning: the PRODIGY architecture
url: local copy of the journal paper (CMU PRODIGY group, JETAI 1995); no stable URL recorded
finding: Learning control rules helps but is not magic. In the logistics domain HAMLET was trained on 400 random problems with 1 to 2 goals and got 17 control rules. On 500 test problems (1 to 50 goals) the number of problems left unsolved fell from 218 to 135 and about 72 solutions were better with rules, none worse. Nodes explored fell from 17,204 to 14,306 and total solution length from 3,132 to 2,930. The authors say running time fell 'but not significantly' because matching many rules is costly.
numbers: 500 test problems; unsolved 218 -> 135 (about 38% fewer); nodes 17,204 -> 14,306 (about 17% fewer); time limit 150*(1+mod(goals,10)) s.
limits: The table in the PDF text is jumbled, so row alignment was checked against the totals row only. Own-system benchmark. Training on easy problems, test on harder ones.
agent_relevance: Real but modest gains from learned search control on top of means-ends planning. Do not expect large speed-ups; watch rule-matching cost (utility problem).

source: Veloso, Carbonell, Perez, Borrajo, Fink & Blythe (1995) Integrating planning and learning: the PRODIGY architecture
url: local copy of the journal paper (CMU PRODIGY group, JETAI 1995); no stable URL recorded
finding: The authors report a failed assumption: explanation-based learning methods built for linear PRODIGY2.0 did not carry over to nonlinear PRODIGY4.0. In nonlinear planning 'it is not feasible to obtain a perfect explanation of why some decisions are correct', so they switched to learning from stored planning cases replayed by analogy. They also removed hidden control knowledge from domain encodings, which hurt performance at first but made learning easier later.
numbers: No numbers given for the failed transfer.
quote: it is not feasible to obtain a perfect explanation of why some decisions are correct
limits: Statement by the system's authors.
agent_relevance: Learned subgoal knowledge should be stored as cases with their evidence, not as proofs. Matches the idea of a subgoal library filled from real impasses.

source: Hewitt (1969) PLANNER: a language for proving theorems in robots
finding: PLANNER is a goal-directed language: goals are created and automatically dismissed when satisfied, procedures give 'recommendations' about which theorem to use and in what order, and assertions can be protected from interference by other procedures. Newell and Simon (1976) list PLANNER as a descendant of GPS.
numbers: Only the summary and preface were read; the rest of the PDF was not examined in detail.
limits: Thin reading, so the finding is limited to the paper's own summary.
agent_relevance: Control by recommendations (which method first) and protection of goals are the two ideas later reused in planners. Weak evidence for us.

source: Schmalhofer & Polson (1986) A production system model for human problem solving (Psychological Research 48:113-122)
finding: Experiment 1 tested whether people keep a fixed 'noticing order' of possible moves, as the Jeffries et al. (1977) river-crossing model assumed. 120 college students solved the (5,3) task (5 missionaries, 5 cannibals, boat for 3; called hobbits and orcs in this experiment). Groups of 40 saw the legal moves listed in one order, in another means-ends order, or no list. The list changed nothing.
numbers: Legal moves per subject: 27.85, 27.88, 27.10 for the three groups. Illegal moves 6.70, 4.28, 5.75. All F < 1. Move-transition correlations between control and each experimental group above .95. Move times also did not differ.
quote: subjects ignored the information on the right half of the screen altogether.
limits: One lab, one problem size for Exp 1 (the second experiment tested the model on (3,2), (4,3) and (5,3), but its numbers were not seen in the extracted text). Subjects may have simply ignored the display, which the authors say.
agent_relevance: People do not appear to use a fixed internal list of operators in order. The step 'list operators, then choose' may be wrong for people; for our agent a stable noticing order would be a design choice, not a copy of humans.

source: Schmalhofer & Polson (1986) A production system model for human problem solving (Psychological Research 48:113-122)
finding: Their production system model has 11 productions, 6 parameters and an illegal-move filter. It splits into move generation, evaluation and execution. People are said to hold two partial strategies that are not merged: a balance strategy (keep missionaries and cannibals even so cannibals never outnumber) and a means-ends strategy (move all to the goal bank). A probability decides which one fires each step. Evaluation rules include 'avoid the backward move', 'avoid the start state' and a means-ends check.
numbers: Parameters P1 to P7 are firing probabilities. Moves are chosen by the first matching production. Working memory holds the previous move and at most 3 proposed moves.
limits: Fit numbers for Exp 2 were not read. The model has free parameters fitted to data.
agent_relevance: Real solvers mix two strategies that conflict, and probability picks between them. A scaffold with a single clean difference-reduction rule will miss the balance rule that protects constraints. Check constraint-keeping as its own operator.

source: Schmalhofer & Polson (1986) A production system model for human problem solving (Psychological Research 48:113-122)
finding: They state that Greeno (1974) showed GPS is not directly a model of human problem solving, yet psychologists often assume problem solving is GPS-like (models by Atwood and Polson 1976, Jeffries et al. 1977, Simon and Reed 1976). They report that the Jeffries et al. model fit the (3,2) problem but could not account for the (5,3) problem without 'baroque ad hoc assumptions' (Polson and Jeffries 1982, p.397). River-crossing graphs differ: (3,2) is nearly a line, (5,3) bushy with a short linear middle, (4,3) has two disjoint solution paths.
numbers: Problem graph shapes: (3,2) linear; (5,3) bushy with short linear middle; (4,3) two parallel paths with no shared state.
quote: Greeno (1974) has demonstrated that GPS is not directly a model of human problem solving
limits: Secondary statement about other people's results; the first-hand papers (Greeno 1974, Jeffries 1977) were not opened.
agent_relevance: Means-ends models fitted one problem and broke on a differently shaped one. Test our means-ends operator on problems with different state-graph shapes, not on one example.

source: Jeffries, Polson, Razran & Atwood (1977) A process model for Missionaries-Cannibals and other river-crossing problems
finding: Extends the Atwood and Polson (1976) water-jug model to four isomorphs of Missionaries and Cannibals. Three stages: means-ends heuristics, memory for visited states, and illegal-move detection. Changing the cover story did not change the number of legal moves to solution but changed illegal moves a lot.
numbers: Four isomorphs. Cited by 59 (Web of Science). Exact N and move counts not read.
quote: variation in cover story produced no differences in number of legal moves to solution
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Later work (a22) says the model's fixed noticing order failed for (5,3).
agent_relevance: Surface wording changes errors but not the path taken. Our verification step should target rule violations, which depend on wording, not path choice.

source: Greeno (1974) Hobbits and orcs: acquisition of a sequential concept (Cognitive Psychology 6)
finding: As summarised in a search result of the abstract: subjects organise the move sequence into small subsequences, not single moves (supporting Thomas 1974). The organisation looked forward-oriented, in contrast to the backward-oriented organisation of the GPS model. One state with non-all-or-none learning involved an ambiguity about backward moves.
numbers: Numbers not read. Feedback groups differed.
limits: Abstract text only, seen through a search result; full paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Humans learned forward chunks of moves, not backward goal chains. A scaffold that only chains backward may differ from human skill; chunked move sequences (macros) are a candidate.

source: Thomas (1974) An analysis of behavior in the hobbits-orcs problem (Cognitive Psychology 6:257-269)
finding: Known only through secondary notes: people use means-ends analysis at first, but some solution steps move away from the goal (backward moves) and are hard. A later 1980 study on predicting one's own moves in hobbits-orcs found no compelling evidence that people need to look ahead to solve it.
numbers: Not read; no sample sizes.
limits: Secondary and flashcard-level summaries only. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: The detour step (a move that increases the difference) is the documented weak point of difference reduction. We should test our scaffold on tasks where progress needs a temporary setback.

source: Anzai & Simon (1979) The theory of learning by doing (Psychological Review 86:124-140)
finding: Described in Neth and Payne (2002) and in search notes: an adaptive production system that mirrored strategy changes of one person solving the 5-disk Tower of Hanoi. Search notes say it covered 4 attempts, with early simple constraints and a recursive goal strategy by the third attempt. VanLehn (1991) reanalysed the protocol and said the participant was 'acting like a scientist'. Solvers often start with guided trial and error and end with a recursive strategy.
numbers: One participant; 4 attempts at 5 disks (from secondary text).
limits: Primary paper not opened. One participant only. Neth and Payne found no sign of deliberate learning moves in groups (a27).
agent_relevance: Strategy can change within one solver across attempts from search to goal recursion. This is the human model for a subgoal library that grows from episodes.

source: Neth & Payne (2002) Thinking by doing? Epistemic actions in the Tower of Hanoi
finding: Experiment with 44 first-year students on six 5-disk ToH problems in four groups (2 instructions x 2 device modes). Device mode: 'exploratory mode' let people try move sequences that were undone and not counted. Groups with it solved with fewer counted moves on trials 4 to 6 (Group 3 vs Group 1, p = .008), but used more total moves (68.7 vs 55.1, not significant). The instruction to minimise only on the last 3 trials did not make people explore early (interaction F(1,20) = .44, p = .51).
numbers: N = 44. Optimal 31 moves. Learning over trials F(5,200) = 16.3. Effectiveness ratios per trial of an exploratory move: 0.5, 0.3, 1.0, 0.2, 1.1, 0.7, no trend.
quote: strong evidence for one sub-type of epistemic action (acting-to-plan) but no evidence for a second sub-type (acting-to-learn).
limits: Cardiff students, one puzzle. Groups were assigned by arrival order and may differ in skill (the authors say so). Group 2 beat Group 1 without exploring, likely by effort (move rate interaction F(1,20) = 18.3).
agent_relevance: Look-ahead by cheap trial and undo helps within a problem. For us: a sandbox/undo step before commit supports planning (matches the 'leaping before you look' flaw).

source: Neth & Payne (2002) Thinking by doing? Epistemic actions in the Tower of Hanoi
finding: People used the explore-and-undo mode only when it paid off immediately. Group 3 used it throughout; Group 4 (told to minimise only on trials 4 to 6) used it more late (F(1,20) = 5.4, p = .03). They did not invest early moves to learn the puzzle. The authors cite O'Hara and Payne (1998) and Trudel and Payne (1995) that rationing actions can make people plan more and learn more.
numbers: Use of epistemic moves: Group 3 fell over time; Group 4 rose in the second half.
limits: Small groups (about 11 each); the instruction manipulation was weak.
agent_relevance: Learning in solvers is mostly a by-product of solving, not deliberate. Our agent should not rely on 'explore to learn' in the same run; store lessons only from real failures.

source: Fansher, Shah & Helie (undated manuscript) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: Experiment 1 (undergraduates, final n = 129): everyone did a 4-disk then a 5-disk Tower of Hanoi, either on a computer (external display) or mentally. Finishing in 15 min was more likely with the computer: 4-disk 100% vs 91% (chi2(1) = 4.45, p = .03); 5-disk 93% vs 63% (B = -2.67, p = .001). But the mental group solved the 5-disk in fewer moves (B = -.47, p = .04). So an external display helped completion and speed while internal work gave better move economy.
numbers: Optimal moves 15 (4 disks) and 31 (5 disks). Move score = (moves - optimal)/optimal. 5-disk finishers: mental n = 39, computer n = 62. Experiment 2 is a pre-registered replication on Prolific workers.
quote: external representations encourage speed while internal representations promote accuracy when solving recursion problems.
limits: Year not stated in the manuscript. Not about means-ends directly. Online and student samples.
agent_relevance: Making the state visible raises completion; forcing mental tracking raises planning. For the scaffold: always keep an explicit state record in code (cheap), but do not let it turn search into blind trial and error.

source: Fansher, Shah & Helie (undated manuscript) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: Strategy self-reports: people who solved only mentally reported remembering move sequences more than computer-only people (.34 vs .22; interaction F(4,315) = 2.93, p = .02). Within person, the mental mode brought more use of subgoals (F(1,112) = 4.46, p = .04) and more move-sequence memory (F(1,112) = 33.86, p < .001), and computer mode more trial and error. Solving a first problem mentally lifted progress on a mental second problem (interaction B = 1.71, p = .03). The paper defines goal recursion as solving subgoals or slightly simpler versions of the original problem, and notes transfer of such strategies is often elusive.
numbers: Self-report shares are fractions of strategy use. Completion and progress effects as in a29.
quote: a strategy where one must solve sub-goals or slightly simpler versions of the original problem to reach a solution
limits: Self-reports are weak evidence of true strategy. Transfer effect modest.
agent_relevance: Goal recursion appears when working memory is the bottleneck. Our agent's context is also a bottleneck, so forcing explicit subgoal stacks may help on deep tasks. Measure it.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes & Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi (Cognitive Psychology 17:248-294)
url: n/a (citation from reference lists; not retrieved)
finding: Known here only from citations: isomorphs of Tower of Hanoi that differ in surface rules are solved at very different difficulty, and external representation turns hard cognitive work into perceptual inference (as Fansher et al. cite it). Citation count about 722 (OpenAlex).
numbers: Not read, no numbers recorded. A claim of a large difficulty ratio between isomorphs was searched for and not verified.
limits: Not opened. Do not quote numbers from this entry.
agent_relevance: Same logical structure can be much harder when moves are phrased as changes or carry hidden load. Reformulating the problem (state, moves) can matter more than the search rule.

source: Simon & Reed (1976) Modeling strategy shifts in a problem-solving task (Cognitive Psychology 8:86-97)
url: n/a (citation from reference lists; not retrieved)
finding: Cited by Schmalhofer and Polson (1986) as one of the GPS-like models of river-crossing. The title says it models shifts of strategy during one task. Citation count about 156 (OpenAlex).
numbers: Not read. No sample size or fit values recorded.
limits: Not opened; page numbers come from an unverified reference list.
agent_relevance: Strategy shift inside a problem (balance idea to goal-directed idea) is the human pattern; our S-state switches could mirror it, triggered by a signal not a timer (G1).

source: Korf (1985) Macro-operators: a weak method for learning (Artificial Intelligence 26:35-77)
finding: From abstract-level notes only: means-ends and subgoal methods work well when subgoals can be solved in order without undoing earlier ones (serial decomposability). Korf proposes macro-operators (stored move sequences) as a learning method for problems where subgoals interfere, such as Rubik's Cube. A later paper says a serially decomposable domain with operator closure has a macro table.

source: Chapman (1987) Planning for conjunctive goals (Artificial Intelligence 32)
finding: From abstract-level notes: Chapman distilled linear and nonlinear planners into one algorithm, TWEAK, proved correct and complete, and argues that all conjunctive planners work in essentially the same way. Linear (non-interleaving) planners cannot solve the Sussman anomaly; interleaving ones can.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: reasoning models and problem complexity (Apple)
finding: On controlled Tower of Hanoi (and three other puzzles) frontier reasoning models show an accuracy collapse past a complexity level. Even when the full Hanoi algorithm was put in the prompt so the model only had to follow it, performance did not improve and collapse came at about the same point. The authors read this as weak step-by-step execution and verification. Three regimes: simple (plain models better), medium (thinking helps), high (both collapse).
numbers: Hanoi minimum moves 2^n - 1. Per-N solution accuracy curves in Fig 7 (N = 1 to 10). Exact collapse N per model not read here.
quote: even when we provide the algorithm in the prompt
limits: Contested: critics say token limits and puzzle format explain part of the collapse; that rebuttal was not opened here. Not a means-ends test.
agent_relevance: Giving the model a recursive procedure is not enough; execution must be run by code, with the model only filling slots (matches section 1 of the schema).

source: Newell & Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving (book); read only as quoted in Norvig (1992)
finding: The book's account of means-ends analysis uses the nursery-school example: find the difference (distance), find what changes it (the car), find what is needed (a battery), then what has batteries, then how to communicate (a telephone). Newell and Simon say this classifying by function and moving between ends, needed functions and means is the 'basic system of heuristic of GPS'. Norvig traces the idea to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics (deliberate about means, not ends).
